standard.title: The Women's Movement in Australia
standard.description: the significant events, individuals and groups in the women's movement in Australia, and how they have changed the role and status of women
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied the roles and rights of women in Australia in earlier periods, including WWI and the interwar years, including women's suffrage and wartime roles.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the significant events, individuals and groups in the women's movement in Australia and explain how they have changed the role and status of women.

nodes.label: Legislative and workforce change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate significant events and legislation connected to women's changing roles in the workforce since 1945 and explain how each contributed to change.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two significant events or pieces of legislation related to women's workforce rights since 1945 and explain the change each produced.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate events connected to changing women's roles in the workforce: the repeal of the marriage bar (which had required women to leave the public service upon marriage), the equal pay cases (1969, 1972), the Sex Discrimination Act 1984, the changing nature of women's participation in employment across the post-war decades, and the persistent gender pay gap; explain how each development changed — or failed fully to change — the role and status of women in the workforce.
wider: Trace the equal pay campaign from the ACTU's 1969 equal pay case through the 1972 decision and into contemporary gender pay gap debates, examining what the 50-year trajectory reveals about the limits of legislative change in producing substantive equality

Investigate the intersection of First Nations women's experiences with the women's movement — examining how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women's advocacy for rights operated both alongside and in tension with the mainstream women's movement

response_modes.reason: The elaborations list the marriage bar and Sex Discrimination Act as exemplars but the broader pattern — waves of legislative change followed by persistent structural inequality — is the analytical point. Extend across multiple legislative milestones to reveal this pattern.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The longitudinal pattern of legislative change and persistent structural inequality is a transferable analytical concept — relevant to K13 (continuing civil rights efforts) and to the broader question of what kinds of change legislation can and cannot produce.
success_criteria: Identify at least two significant developments in women's workforce rights since 1945 and explain what each changed
Explain what the marriage bar was and what its repeal signified
Use evidence to evaluate whether legislative changes produced substantive change in the status of women in the workforce
nodes.notes: Limited width descriptor — only two elaborations. Both are treated at typical_width. Wider items deepen the analysis of workforce change and add the intersectional perspective.

nodes.label: Significant female leaders
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the contributions of significant female leaders in Australian public life and explain how each contributed to changing the role and status of women.
nodes.minimum_width: Investigate the contributions of at least two significant female leaders from different domains and explain what each achieved.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the contributions of significant female leaders across multiple domains: political leaders and activists (e.g. Gough Whitlam's women's policy, Joan Kirner, Carmen Lawrence, Julia Gillard), social reformers, sporting identities, artists and entertainers; explain how each contributed to changing the role and status of women in their domain.
wider: Investigate a female leader whose contribution is less widely recognised — examining how gender, race, or class shaped both their activism and the historical recognition they received

Compare the strategies and contexts of female leaders from different eras (e.g. 1970s second-wave feminists vs contemporary leaders), examining how the nature of gender inequality and the strategies to address it have changed

response_modes.reason: Students need exposure to a range of significant female leaders across different domains and eras to build a genuinely broad picture of the women's movement — not just the most prominent political figures.

success_criteria: Describe the contributions of at least two significant female leaders from different domains
Explain how each leader's contribution changed the role or status of women in their domain
Evaluate the extent to which individual leadership — as opposed to collective movement or legislative action — drove change in women's status
